$$

The particle's velocity in the $y$-direction is given by ${y}^{′}(t).$ Therefore, the acceleration in the $y$-direction is ${y}^{″}(t):$

Differentiating ${y}^{′}(t)$ using the quotient rule, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{6-12{t}^{2}}{2{t}^{3}+3t}\right) \\  & =\frac{(-24t)(2{t}^{3}+3t)-(6-12{t}^{2})(6{t}^{2}+3)}{(2{t}^{3}+3t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-48{t}^{4}-72{t}^{2}-36{t}^{2}-18+72{t}^{4}+36{t}^{2}}{(2{t}^{3}+3t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{24{t}^{4}-72{t}^{2}-18}{(2{t}^{3}+3t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(4{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}-3)}{(2{t}^{3}+3t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=1,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(1) & =\frac{6(4(1)^{4}-12(1)^{2}-3)}{(2(1)^{3}+3(1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-11)}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{66}{25}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration in the $y$-direction when $t=1$ is $-\frac{66}{25}\,\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2}.$

17592186541078.question/worked-solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

In parts 1 and 2, we found

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}},\,{y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2.
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
{t}^{2}-2=0\,⟹\,t=\pm \sqrt{2}.
$$

Note that $-\sqrt{2}\notin (0,\infty ),$ so we only consider the value $t=\sqrt{2}.$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(\sqrt{2})=\frac{5}{27}\ne 0,
$$

which confirms that the curve's tangent is horizontal when $t=\sqrt{2}.$
